title: Brand voice for a technical product
metaTitle: Brand voice for a technical product
excerpt: Technical buyers forgive plain language. They do not forgive vagueness. Write the way a careful engineer explains a tool to a colleague who has to use it.
alt: A cream sofa between two bright windows, with a framed abstract painting and teal vases, a calm room for an article about speaking plainly to technical buyers.
caption: A quiet room, with the objects easy to name. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How should a technical product sound?
faqs.answer: Sound like a careful colleague explaining a tool. Name the object, the action, and the result. Skip the costume of innovation. A buyer who lives in the product all day will trust a plain sentence and will remember a vague one, because they have to unpack it on a call with their own team.

faqs.question: Can the marketing site be warmer than the app?
faqs.answer: It can have more air, and it should use the same nouns as the interface. If the site says hub and the app says workspace, the voice has already split. Warmth is a matter of courtesy and specificity. It is not a second vocabulary invented for the homepage.

faqs.question: Where should the voice be written down?
faqs.answer: Write three sentences you will say, and three you will not, plus the names of the primary objects. Put that page where marketing, product, and support all edit. A long adjective list will not survive a Thursday. The sentences will, if they can be used in a button, an error, and a homepage line.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Brand voice for saas, when the buyer is technical, is a way of explaining a tool to a colleague. Plain language is welcome. Vagueness is not. They will forgive a simple sentence. They will not forgive a sentence they have to translate before they can tell whether the product fits.

Write the way you would speak in a working session. Name the object. Name the action. Say what happens next. Leave the costume of innovation for companies that are selling a feeling.

## Plain is a form of respect

A technical reader is often the person who will be asked, later, "does this actually do the thing." They are skimming for a claim they can defend. "Export the Friday report without the extra column" is a claim. "Unlock seamless operational excellence" is a job you handed them. They will either invent a meaning or close the tab.

[Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) on visits is blunt about the time you get. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and a value proposition has to be clear within about 10 seconds to earn a longer look. They also read only about a quarter of the words on the pages they do open. The sentence that survives is the one in the first screen, in words a colleague would accept. Everything else is optional.

[People-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether the content demonstrates a real understanding of the audience. For this audience, understanding looks like precision. You know the job. You know the failure. You do not dress the failure up as a journey. A page that could describe any tool in the category has not understood them yet.

Hanabi's own public line, clarity over complexity, is a useful test even if your product is dense. Density can be the point, as it is for a trading screen or an ops ledger. The voice can still be clear. Clear means a person can say what the control does. It does not mean the screen must be empty.

## Sentences you will say, and sentences you will not

Write three sentences the product is willing to publish. Full sentences, with a subject and a claim. "Admins can see which invites have not been accepted." "The export matches the columns on screen." "If a payment fails, we say which field to fix." A teammate should be able to use these on a homepage, a button's neighbor, and an error.

Write three you will not say. No "next-generation platform" without the generation's actual difference. No "seamless" as a substitute for the step you removed. No "AI-powered" as weather. If a model does a job, say the job and say what a human still checks. If it does not, do not borrow the word. Technical readers have heard it used as perfume. They will discount the next sentence too.

Test the sentences in the interface, not only on the site. An error that says "Something went wrong" after a homepage that was specific is a costume change. An error that names the field and the fix is the same company under stress. Empty states and success messages belong in the same test. Voice that only exists on the marketing page is a campaign, not a brand.

Read them to someone who uses a competing tool. If they ask "which product," you were specific. If they nod politely, you wrote a category. Categories are where budgets go to compare spreadsheets. A specific sentence is how you stay out of the wrong row.

## One vocabulary across the site and the product

Pick the nouns and keep them. The thing a customer has many of. The action that creates one. The person who can invite. Write the list down, twelve words or fewer, and use it in the nav, the docs, the changelog, and the sales page. A glossary that marketing does not read will not save you. A short list pinned in the repo will.

Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai are public product interfaces with a point of view. The lesson for voice is that a screen can be specific without narrating itself. Buttons do a lot of the brand work. If the button is precise, the homepage can be precise too. If the button is vague, no headline will rescue the day the user is stuck.

Docs should start from the job, in this voice. "Invite a teammate" rather than "Team resource overview." The changelog should say what the user can now do, not the name of the refactor. Support replies should be allowed to paste the docs. If they have to rewrite them, the voice manual failed, and the rewrite is the draft you should have shipped.

A second audience, such as an executive buyer who will not live in the tool, still deserves the same nouns. You can add a sentence of consequence for them. "Your ops lead stops rebuilding the Friday sheet." You should not invent a parallel product name to sound strategic. The executive will forward your page to the technical buyer. The nouns have to survive that forward.

## What warmth is allowed to be

Warmth is courtesy and specificity. "You can leave this for tomorrow. Drafts stay in the account." That is warm. "We're so excited you're here" is a delay, and on a technical product it sounds like the tool is not ready to talk about itself. Excitement is not information. Information, delivered without contempt, is the warmth this reader recognizes.

Humor is allowed when the task is intact. A small human note in an empty state can work if the action is still obvious. A joke that replaces the instruction will be the thing they remember, and not in the way you hoped. In an incident, drop the humor. Status copy should be plain enough to paste into their own incident channel.

Do not talk down. "Simply click here" is a small insult when the step is not simple. If it is simple, you do not need the adverb. If it is not, "simply" is a lie. Say the step. Say the catch. Respect is the tone. Adjectives are not.

Contrast is part of voice, in the literal sense too. Body text has to be readable. A whisper-grey sentence on a marketing page, chosen because it felt refined, fails the colleague who is skimming on a phone in daylight. The words you worked on should be possible to read. Refinement that hides the claim is just vagueness with better type.

## A page the whole team will open

Keep the voice note short enough to use.

1. Who we are talking to, in one line.
2. Three sentences we will say.
3. Three we will not.
4. The noun list.
5. One example of an error, an empty state, and a homepage line.

Put it where engineers will open it. A markdown file next to the UI strings beats a brand PDF in a drive nobody shares. If you have a client portal, keep a copy there too, so the decision survives a team change. The note is done when a new writer can produce a button label without a meeting.

Review strings the way you review code. A pull request that changes "Export" to "Generate artifact" is a voice change. It needs a reason. The homepage, the email, and the doc that say Export have to move together, or you have created a scavenger hunt. Own that checklist. Voice drifts in the gaps between teams, not inside any one of them.

On a Hanabi project the sentences are design material, made in Figma beside the screens and then checked in the browser where wrapping and real content tell the truth. Illustrator may hold a mark. It should not hold the only copy of the words. Words live where the product lives.

## Voice in the hard moments

The hard moments are the brand. A failed payment. A permissions wall. A partial outage. A changelog entry that removes a field people liked. Write these before you write another feature announcement. You will not have the calm to invent them on the day, and the default copy from a framework will not sound like you.

Say what happened, what the person can do, and what you do not know yet. That structure is the same one a good status page uses, and it is the same one a careful engineer uses in a incident thread. Your product should be welcome in that thread. If your sentences would embarrass the person pasting them, rewrite them now.

Do not use the hard moment to restate the mission. They know why they bought you, or they are about to forget, and a mission paragraph will not help them fix the field. One sentence of orientation is plenty. Then the action. Then the link to the longer note if they want it.

Collect the phrases support already uses, the ones customers reply to with "thanks, that worked." Those phrases are the voice. Promote them into the product. Retire the ones that create a second round of questions. This is research you already paid for, sitting in the inbox.

## The limit of a voice document

A document will not fix a product that does not do what the sentence says. If you cannot export the Friday report, do not write the sentence yet. Voice that outruns the software is a kind of vagueness with better grammar. Ship the behavior, or narrow the claim. Technical readers check.

A document also will not unify two companies that were never one idea. If the marketing site is a carnival and the product is a ledger, start with the sentence you are willing to repeat, then change the surfaces that break it. Adjectives will not paper over that seam. The next practical step is often the names of the pages themselves, because a clever title hides the offer this voice just worked to make plain.

That naming problem is the next piece. [Naming pages the way buyers search](/blog/naming-pages-the-way-buyers-search) is about titles a technical buyer can find and forward. Read it when the sentences are true and the navigation still speaks in internal poetry.

If you want to see product surfaces where the words and the interface carry the same idea, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The test is whether a colleague could explain the screen after one look, without apologizing for the copy.
